newsitem.title: USA: European firm sent deadly chemical to Haiti-lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: European firm sent deadly chemical to Haiti-lawsuit.

text.p: More than 70 children in Haiti may have been killed by taking cough syrup tainted with a deadly chemical in sweetener shipped by a European chemical company, a lawyer said on Tuesday.

The Pan American Health Organization said last year at least 49 children had died from kidney failure linked to the syrup. But Miami attorney David Mishael said Haitian authorities had told him at least 85 children were treated after taking the syrup and at least 70 had died.
The final toll might never be known because many people in rural Haiti would not have sought treatment, he said.

A product liability lawsuit filed in a U.S. District Court last Thursday alleged that Helm A.G. of Hamburg, Germany, and its Netherlands-based distribution unit, Vos B.V., were negligent in shipping glycerin contaminated with a chemical used in anti-freeze to a drug company in Haiti.
The chemical, used to sweeten an anti-fever medication, caused a "mass poisoning which caused the deaths of hundreds of children," the lawsuit contended.
Mishael, who filed the suit on behalf of the families of 35 victims, would not confirm a published report that he would seek $100 million in damages.

The lawsuit alleged that Helm and Vos tested, labeled and warranted the glycerin as "pharmaceutical grade" with a 98 percent minimum purity and shipped it to Pharval Laboratories in Haiti, where it was used to make two liquid cold syrups, Afebrile and Valodon.

The glycerin, manufactured in China, was at least 25 percent diethylene glycol, a toxic chemical used in lacquers and anti-freeze, the lawsuit said. Investigations by U.S. agencies found that the contamination occurred before the glycerin reached Haiti.

Children who took the cold medication developed brain damage and their kidneys failed, Mishael said. Those who survived were left with "catastrophic physical injuries requiring lifetime medical treatment."
A spokesman for Helm U.S. of Piscataway, New Jersey, the U.S. subsidiary of Helm A.G., said the company and its Vos unit would have no immediate comment on the lawsuit.

Vos ordered the glycerin through Metall-Chemie, a Hamburg-based chemical trader, which then ordered the chemical from Sinochem, a trading company in China, the lawsuit said. Drums of glycerin were shipped in December 1994 from Xingang, China, to Vos in Rotterdam.

Vos used "an inferior method to test the glycerin," certifying it as 98 percent pure and instructing employees to obliterate the original labels to conceal identification of the original manufacturer, a practice known as "neutralization," the lawsuit alleged.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and the Food and Drug Administration investigated the poisonings but have yet to find exactly how the product became tainted.

U.S. law allowed the suit to be filed in a federal court if no remedy could be obtained in the jurisdiction where the incident occurred and the Haitian judiciary was ill-equipped to deal with such a case, Mishael said.
